title: The three branches
note: Drafted for Prompt 12 (Unit 2). Every lesson is a draft until a person reviews it (content/course/README.md).

listen.explanationKey: Name the three branches of government.
facts: The federal government has three branches: legislative, executive and judicial.
Congress is the legislative branch. The President leads the executive branch. The courts are the judicial branch.
Each branch has its own job, so no one branch has all the power.

newWords.meaning: the branch that carries out the laws
the branch that makes the laws

story.say: The federal government has three branches: legislative, executive and judicial.

help.simpler: The national government has three parts. Each part is called a branch.
help.example: A tree has branches. The government also splits into branches.
help.why: The test asks you to name the three branches.

help.simpler: Congress is the part of the government that makes laws.
help.example: “Legislative” comes from an old word for law.
help.why: Congress is one answer when the test asks for the three branches.

story.say: The President leads the executive branch.

help.simpler: The President is in charge of the executive branch.
help.example: “Execute” means to carry out. The executive branch carries out the laws.
help.why: The test asks which branch the President is in charge of. The answer is the executive branch.

story.say: The courts are the judicial branch.

help.simpler: The courts, including the Supreme Court, make up the judicial branch.
help.example: “Judicial” sounds like “judge.” Judges work in the courts.
help.why: The courts are the third branch on the test.

check.prompt: Which branch does the President lead?

story.say: Each branch has its own job, so no one branch has all the power.

help.simpler: Each part does a different job. No part can do everything.
help.example: Congress makes laws, the President carries them out, and the courts explain them.
help.why: This is the idea of checks and balances from Unit 1.

check.statement: One branch has all the power.

readIt.sentence: Who is the President of the United States?

writeIt.sentence: The President is in the White House.

listen.explanationKey: Who signs bills to become laws?
facts: A bill is an idea for a new law. Congress writes and passes bills.
The President signs a bill to make it a law.
The President can also veto a bill. Veto means saying no to it.

newWords.meaning: an idea for a new law, written by Congress
to write your name to say yes
when the President says no to a bill
when Congress passes a bill again after a veto, with two-thirds of both parts. They go against the president to pass or veto a law.

story.say: A bill is an idea for a new law.

help.simpler: A bill is a plan for a law. It is not a law yet.
help.example: A bill might say that drivers must stop for school buses.
help.why: You need the word “bill” for two test questions.

help.simpler: Congress writes bills and votes on them.
help.example: If most of Congress votes yes, the bill passes and goes to the President.
help.why: Bills start in Congress, the lawmaking branch.

check.statement: A bill is already a law.

story.say: The President signs a bill to make it a law.

help.simpler: When the President signs a bill, it becomes a law.
help.example: The President signs it with a pen, and the new law can begin.
help.why: The test asks who signs bills to become laws. The answer is the President.

story.say: The President can also veto a bill.

help.simpler: The President can refuse to sign a bill.
help.example: The President works in the White House, where bills arrive to be signed or vetoed.
help.why: The test asks who vetoes bills. The answer is the President.

story.say: Veto means saying no to it.

help.example: After a veto, the bill does not become law, unless two-thirds of both parts of Congress vote for it again.
help.why: This is one way the branches check each other.

check.prompt: Tap the step where the President signs the bill.

writeIt.sentence: The President lives in Washington, D.C.
